summary: Polar Horizon is a free browser tool for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates by where the Sun and Earth sit against each site's real horizon. Pick Artemis III candidate regions or type any coordinates, choose a day, month or year, and it ranks sites by sunlight for power, direct-to-Earth link time, the longest dark spell and the battery needed to survive it. A 360° sky view draws the actual terrain skyline, traced from NASA LOLA elevation data, with the Sun and Earth moving across it. A timeline shows when each site has power, a link, both or neither. Positions come from standard astronomical formulas and agree with NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.031°. The result is striking: on a smooth Moon, Connecting Ridge would sit in darkness for 113 days in 2027. With real terrain, its longest dark spell is 2.1 days. It runs from one web page, with no login or install.
details:
Sun and Moon positions follow Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms (chapters 25, 47 and 53), including the Moon's libration. For each site the tool computes the Sun's and Earth's elevation and direction as seen from the surface, and the share of the Sun's disc above the horizon. The horizon is real terrain: from each site the tool traces outward in every degree of direction, up to 250 km, over NASA LOLA elevation data, allowing for the Moon's curvature, and keeps the highest angle. The Sun and Earth count only when they clear that skyline. A switch turns terrain off to compare with a smooth Moon.

One HTML file: plain JavaScript and Canvas 2D. No backend, no build step, no install. Hosted on GitHub Pages. The NASA elevation grid (833 × 833 heights) is built into the page.

Instead of a static lighting map, the tool shows the sky from the lander's point of view: the real terrain skyline with the Sun skimming along it and Earth rising and setting with libration. Anyone can add their own coordinates and get a terrain horizon instantly. A one-click comparison with a smooth Moon shows why terrain decides everything at the pole.

Mission planners can screen sites and dates in seconds before detailed studies. Educators can show why the pole has near-constant sunlight on high ridges but a monthly Earth blackout. The public can follow Artemis landing regions with a tool that needs no login. Results are checked against NASA JPL Horizons, and those NASA points are drawn on the chart so anyone can see the match.

Code, layout, data processing scripts and text were written with Anthropic's Claude (Claude Code) and reviewed and tested by the team. No AI-generated images, video or audio. The screenshots are real captures of the tool. No NASA logos, flags or branding are used anywhere.
